a351.speaker: Somalia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (statement)
a351.speech: Strongly condemned the attack on the residence of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) ambassador in Khartoum, calling it a violation of international law and a serious breach of diplomatic norms; in a statement, the ministry urged all nations to uphold the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which guarantees the safety and sanctity of diplomatic missions; Somalia emphasized the need for international laws to be respected to maintain the security and dignity of embassies, especially in conflict zones like Sudan.

a351.speaker: United Arab Emirates (government)
a351.speech: On Monday, the UAE reported that a Sudanese military aircraft targeted the ambassador's residence in Khartoum, causing significant damage; the UAE plans to raise formal complaints with the United Nations, the African Union, and the League of Arab States.

a351.speaker: UAE Foreign Ministry
a351.speech: Condemned the incident as a "heinous attack" and demanded accountability from the Sudanese military.

a351.speaker: United Arab Emirates (government)
a351.speech: Insists that it is committed to de-escalation and humanitarian assistance, despite accusations that it is arming the RSF.

a351.speaker: United Nations
a351.speech: The United Nations estimates that nearly 25 million people, half of Sudan's population, now require humanitarian aid, while over 8 million have fled their homes.

a351.speaker: U.N. sanctions monitors
a351.speech: Have deemed the accusations that the UAE is arming the RSF credible, pointing to evidence of arms transfers through Chad.

a351.speaker: Sudanese military
a351.speech: Has consistently pointed to the UAE's alleged support as a factor in prolonging the conflict.

a355.speaker: An unnamed maize farmer (man in his forties), Gahongore hill, Bubanza
a355.speech: Testified: "These caterpillars are ravaging our maize fields. They attack the stalks and the leaves." ; "Were it not for these caterpillars, maize growing is productive and profitable." ; said he had invested more than 2 million BIF in maize growing, half of it borrowed from a local microfinance institution which he had hoped to repay after the harvest, and that he cannot see by what magic wand he will repay his loan; he estimates his lost earnings at five million BIF this season.

a355.speaker: An unnamed maize farmer (man in his forties), Gahongore hill, Bubanza
a355.speech: Said he is worried about his family's future: "Maize farming is my only livelihood," and wondered how his family will keep meeting its needs; he also testified that the majority of the population lives from maize and rice farming.

a355.speaker: Jacques Nkengurutse, maize farmer on Gahongore hill
a355.speech: Agreed: "These caterpillars threaten the survival of many inhabitants of this locality," adding that most of them live from maize farming, which is less costly than rice growing, which requires enormous financial means.

a355.speaker: Jacques Nkengurutse, maize farmer on Gahongore hill
a355.speech: Said he is worried about the absence of effective pesticides against the caterpillars, which resist many of the pesticides recommended by agricultural authorities; he said he has used them repeatedly with no effect, that the only effective method is to search for the caterpillars in the leaves of each maize plant, and that even if adult caterpillars are killed their eggs remain in the leaves and become caterpillars within a week. He asked those in charge of the agricultural sector to find other, more powerful pesticides, and said he no longer expects much from the harvest after investing 1,500,000 BIF in maize growing.

a355.speaker: J.K., maize farmer on Gahongore hill
a355.speech: Deplored the inaction of the authorities in charge of Agriculture, who are not getting involved in the search for pesticides that kill the caterpillars: "This is the third year in a row that these caterpillars have ravaged our maize fields." ; "It is incomprehensible that caterpillars destroy crops for three years without the authorities being able to find a solution. Even the pesticides available in pharmacies are not effective." He stated that he sprayed his one-hectare maize field with five bottles of pesticide per week with no result, and put his lost earnings at 2,400,000 BIF for the season.

a355.speaker: Administrator of Bubanza commune
a355.speech: Stated that he is aware of the problem, that the armyworms began to appear in 2016 but were no longer the threat they were two years ago, and said he is concerned about another disease also attacking maize which has broken out in the Buvyuko zone of Bubanza commune. He was reassuring: "The administration is doing everything to fight this disease," saying he had already informed the provincial directorate of Agriculture and hopes ministry officials will take all necessary precautions against the new disease.

a420.speaker: World Bank 2024/5 country classification
a420.speech: Considers 22 African countries as low-income and 24 as lower-middle-income.

a420.speaker: Institute for Security Studies' African Futures and Innovation programme (research)
a420.speech: According to its research, only beyond mid-century does the ratio of working-age Africans to dependants enable labour to enhance economic growth.

a420.speaker: Empirical research (cited)
a420.speech: Most empirical research supports the view that capital accumulation (physical capital investment such as infrastructure, machinery, factories and equipment) is the primary driver of growth during the early stages of development.

a530.speaker: Kassim Haroun Ali, Minister of Decentralisation of Djibouti
a530.speech: Expressed his satisfaction at the signing of this Memorandum of Understanding and underlined the importance of the active participation of civil society in the local development process. He declared that "this partnership will strengthen our commitment to the active participation of CSOs in the framework of decentralisation" ; "By improving their capacity," the minister stressed, "we will together be able to better respond to the needs of our communities and promote inclusive and sustainable development."

a530.speaker: Ban Saraf, project head of the Project to Support Civil Society Engagement in the Local Development Process (USAID-funded)
a530.speech: Expressed her enthusiasm for this joint initiative. She declared that "this partnership will allow us to strengthen the voice of local communities and to promote better coordination between CSOs and governmental actors. Together, we will be able to take up local challenges and work towards a better future for all."

a534.speaker: Badabouè Florent Bazié, Governor of the Tannounyan region, Burkina Faso (representing the Minister of Basic Education)
a534.speech: In his address, he insisted on the need for all actors in the education system to redouble their efforts in order to build a school system that is stronger, more accessible and more equitable ; "Every enrolment, every classroom opened, every teacher mobilised is a national victory," the governor recalled, while saluting the determination and courage of teachers who, he said, despite the security challenges, continue to carry out the mission of transmitting knowledge.

a534.speaker: Badabouè Florent Bazié, Governor of the Tannounyan region, Burkina Faso
a534.speech: Took the occasion to invite pupils to discipline and hard work, while inviting parents of pupils to accompany their children in their school careers; he further urged teachers to maintain their patriotic and professional commitment in the service of the Nation.

a534.speaker: Jacques Sosthène Dingara, Minister of Basic Education, Literacy and the Promotion of National Languages of Burkina Faso (message conveyed by the governor)
a534.speech: The minister's message also highlighted the major reforms marking this school year, namely the progressive generalisation from this year of the teaching of English, which will extend to the CE2, CM1 and CM2 classes, the transformation of classic schools into bilingual schools, the promotion of school councils, and the transparent and equitable management of human and financial resources.

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: Said the EU's engagement in Burkina Faso's culture has several segments, one of the most important being the Support Programme for the Creative Industries and the Governance of Culture (PAIC GC), run in Burkina for 5 years at 10 million euros, through which more than 200 actions in culture, the arts, theatre and cinema have been funded, including support for 12 Burkinabe films in competition at FESPACO ; said other platforms enabled support for the International Handicrafts Fair of Ouagadougou (SIAO), the National Culture Week and Les Recreatrales in 2024, and that the EU is finalising a large regional support programme for the arts and culture that will foster intercultural dialogue.

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: Assessed the results as "Very positive", saying there has been a great deal of enthusiasm, that Burkina Faso is a country of artists with an embarrassment of choice, and that there are fantastic artists in the country, a great advantage for cinema and theatre.

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: On FESPACO: "It is a beautiful story with FESPACO. For me it is my first FESPACO. I am astounded and it is incredible. But for the European Union, we have been at the rendezvous for 30 years, and we support the biennale. What we expect is a great success. Because FESPACO remains a flagship event from a continental point of view, from a global point of view." ; said he attended the screening of the film DEMBA which he liked, that he would particularly like to follow "Katanga, la danse des scorpions", and that thanks to FESPACO he has started watching "Bienvenue a Kikideni", which allows people like him who are not Burkinabe to enter into and better understand Burkinabe society.

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: "There are several, but honestly what truly surprised me is that Burkina Faso is a country of artists. I have never encountered a country that is so talented, so gifted, but also so interested in the arts. Even within the Delegation of the European Union we have several artists such as photographers and writers, and it is really very impressive."

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: On plans for 8 March: said gender is a cross-cutting dimension found in all EU programmes, actions and projects, integral to areas of intervention such as health, education and infrastructure; that for 8 March 2025 the delegation will go to the green belt of Ouagadougou where the EU has set up development projects for women such as market gardening and weaving, to meet these women and assess the impact of EU support; and that "We only accompany and try to help, but above all, it is these women who were already taking charge of themselves... they are really incredible women. We are only helping, because it is really they who are going to do the work."

a547.speaker: Daniel Aristi Gaztelumendi, Ambassador of the European Union to Burkina Faso
a547.speech: "The European Union is very present here in Burkina and we work in many different fields with our Burkinabe colleagues. I can mention education, health, infrastructure, job creation, agriculture, and also humanitarian aid."

a547.speaker: Robert Alan Aurthur (quoted by the EU Ambassador)
a547.speech: As Robert Alan Aurthur used to say, cultural differences should not separate people; we should not speak of difference, but of diversity, and brought together we make a great strength for humanity.

a573.speaker: Mohamed Abdoulkader Moussa Helem, Minister of Environment and Sustainable Development of Djibouti
a573.speech: Expressed his wish to strengthen cooperation between Djibouti and the UN organisation in the field of the environment and sustainable development; noted that his ministerial department is concerned with preserving natural ecosystems such as forests, water bodies and biodiversity, confronting environmental pollution, sustainable development and the management of natural resources, in addition to promoting environmental awareness and education and combating climate change.

a679.speaker: Patrick Pouyanne, Chief Executive of TotalEnergies
a679.speech: Expressed confidence as recently as July 2024 in a Bloomberg report that Namibia would experience an oil boom similar to that of Guyana ; stated that achieving acceptable production costs is a challenge given the high costs of re-injecting gas.

a679.speaker: Maggy Shino, Namibian Petroleum Commissioner
a679.speech: Quoted by Bloomberg via OilNOW: "We are preparing the country to become an energy hub for the region."

a679.speaker: Maggy Shino, Namibian Petroleum Commissioner
a679.speech: Stated, according to a recent Reuters report, that the government is working with the operators, including Shell, TotalEnergies and Galp, on developing a joint infrastructure plan that may include an expanded version of the Kudu gas-to-power project.

a679.speaker: Bloomberg (report)
a679.speech: Forecast that Namibia's economy could potentially double or triple by 2027.

a679.speaker: Reuters (report)
a679.speech: Recent report cited as the source for the Namibian government working with operators on a joint infrastructure plan, which could delay production into the 2030s.

a679.speaker: ReconAfrica (Reconnaissance Energy Africa Ltd.)
a679.speech: Reports that the company is making good progress with the Naingopo exploration well targeting the Otavi carbonate reservoir with an estimated 181 million barrels of oil or 937 billion cubic feet of natural gas; says the project has been delayed because of "technical adjustments" but that it still expects to reach the target depth of 3,800 metres, with results expected after a comprehensive log analysis.

a679.speaker: Civil society groups, activists and environmental experts
a679.speech: Continue to criticise ReconAfrica's exploration in the ecologically sensitive KAZA area and have repeatedly demanded an immediate halt to these activities because of potential environmental impacts on wildlife and water resources, and thus on the local population and ecosystems.

a692.speaker: World Bank
a692.speech: According to the World Bank, Malawi receives approximately 40% of its national budget from foreign aid.

a716.speaker: Botswana Nurses Union (BONU)
a716.speech: Expressed shock and disbelief over the move, saying it will affect those already on HIV treatment.

a716.speaker: Peter Baleseng, President, Botswana Nurses Union (BONU)
a716.speech: Emphasised that it is incomprehensible for patients undergoing Highly Active Anti-Retroviral Therapy (HAART) to miss their treatments, while holding out hope that the Americans can successfully block Trump’s harmful agenda ; "This is not only a dangerous motive but an unethical one" ; "To subject human lives to such uncertainty is simply unacceptable."

a716.speaker: Ministry of Health of Botswana
a716.speech: Stated that the move will have an impact on the delivery of health in the country.

a716.speaker: Dr Christopher Nyanga, Spokesperson, Ministry of Health of Botswana
a716.speech: Explained that just like other countries, Botswana has been fortunate to receive generous aid from the government of the United States of America for many decades ; "In the health sector, this aid comprised funding for direct service delivery and technical support, which has over the years been instrumental to the growth of the health sector of this country."

a812.speaker: Genscher Mbwabwa, Lilongwe City Council director of commerce
a812.speech: “Indeed there is still an amount of over K13 billion to be collected by the council and we are doing all we can to collect it. We are optimistic that it will be collected,” responded the council’s director of commerce.

a812.speaker: Genscher Mbwabwa, Lilongwe City Council director of commerce
a812.speech: “The MCA project will indeed help us in revenue collection improvement especially in land-based revenue collection from plot identification, documentation, valuation and others. The whole of this process will be automated,” Mbwabwa said.

a812.speaker: Lilongwe City Council
a812.speech: According to the council, the capital city is currently enduring a 15 percent vendors’ growth rate with an estimated number of registered vendors at over 10,000 and 6,000 shops, numbers explained by the rapid population growth and high unemployment rates; the council sees this as a revenue opportunity and hopes that modernising revenue systems would push the revenue to around K15 billion annually.

a812.speaker: Cosmas Chigwe, financial expert
a812.speech: Said city and district councils should be able to sustain themselves without being supported by the Central Government on operations, challenging them to be more inventive and innovative; cited efforts being made by Nkhotakota District Council, which has been seen investing in commercial ventures to expand revenue base, planning to issue municipal bonds while intensifying revenue collection. “These councils would need to be supported by the Central Government if they were more inventive and creative. I’m not sure about their expenditure lines but I don’t think they have too much to pay for,” Chigwe said.

a825.speaker: Modibo Tounkara, voluntary early-retiree (partant volontaire à la retraite anticipée), in a letter to the newsroom
a825.speech: Alerts the authorities once again to the ordeal of his fellow voluntary retirees and their dependants, recalling that “full of development initiatives and convinced of Mali’s economic revival, we accepted the first voluntary retirement programme, financed by USAID (the United States of America)” and that other waves followed with the World Bank; says that once the installation allowance was used up very few projects were financed, the State used the rest of the funds and the retirees were left without follow-up by the State, the trade union, political leaders, civil society and the donors (the United States of America and the World Bank) ; says the most worrying paradox, which undermines the morality of the State, is that the framework agreement on early retirement concluded between the State and the financial partners (USAID and the World Bank) remains untraceable in all the national archives.

a825.speaker: Modibo Tounkara, voluntary early-retiree (partant volontaire à la retraite anticipée), in a letter to the newsroom
a825.speech: Denounces what he calls a “genocide” of thousands of patriotic officials “deceived by their country and by Western imperialism”, says other African countries accepted “this vicious early retirement programme (designed to destabilise Africa)” at much better rates and settled the problem honourably, while in Mali “the State’s bad faith is obvious”; accuses the UNTM trade union confederation of only pretending to be at the retirees’ side, and asks: “Is this sound justice, or democracy?”

a825.speaker: Modibo Tounkara, voluntary early-retiree (partant volontaire à la retraite anticipée), in a letter to the newsroom
a825.speech: Appeals to President Assimi Goita: “In the name of GOD who knows all and can do all, please render justice, Mr President Assimi Goita, for such a tiny but citizen-minded part of your people”; asks that, if their entitlements are too large in this period of crisis, the State pay a lump-sum consolation payment in addition to the social pension to allow them to enrol in Social Security, and says he ardently hopes this will take effect in January 2023; asks that the national justice system examine their case.

a825.speaker: Choguel Maiga, Prime Minister of Mali
a825.speech: Made a declaration recognising the retirees’ rights with the State, but afterwards there was a blackout, according to the letter.

a825.speaker: Ahmed Sekou Toure, first President of the Republic of Guinea Conakry (quoted)
a825.speech: “I prefer dignity in poverty to opulence in slavery.”

a896.speaker: Precious Chinyama, National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) senior disease control officer
a896.speech: “We have a lot of work to do because we are continuing to register a lot of malaria cases in our country.”

a896.speaker: Precious Chinyama, National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) senior disease control officer
a896.speech: Said in 2022 the malaria incidence was 202 per 1000 population, but it increased to 328 per 1000 population in 2023 and jumped to 467 per 1000 population in 2024; said that prior to 2022 the numbers were on a steady decrease from 2020, prompting the Ministry of Health to set an ambitious goal of eliminating malaria as a public health concern in Malawi by 2030, as outlined in the National Malaria Strategic Plan covering 2023-2030 ; said various factors contributed to the rise in malaria cases between 2022 and 2024, including disasters the country experienced during that period, and the wearing out of distributed mosquito nets ; feared that the actual number of cases in the country could be more than the recorded figures, saying there are some incidents that are not reported.

a896.speaker: Precious Chinyama, National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) senior disease control officer
a896.speech: Added that funding cuts are also a threat to the fight against malaria ; “Since we had a lot of cases in 2024, we spent a lot of resources on treatment which will also affect availability of resources.”

a896.speaker: Precious Chinyama, National Malaria Control Programme (NMCP) senior disease control officer
a896.speech: Was hopeful that the recent distribution of about 11.7 million nets completed in June 2025 will help contain the sharp rise in malaria cases, and called on the private sector to support the fight against malaria, saying eliminating the disease requires collaborative efforts.

a896.speaker: National Malaria Control Programme statistics (presented at the NAPPPAM annual general meeting)
a896.speech: Show the number of malaria cases rose from 4.6 million in 2022 to 6.491 million in 2023 and to 9.470 million in 2024, and that the number of malaria deaths rose from 1 670 in 2023 to 2 252 in 2024.

a896.speaker: Ministry of Health data (Malawi)
a896.speech: Shows that implementation of the National Malaria Strategic Plan was already facing an average financing gap of 51 percent for the first four years (2023-2027) even before the latest donor pullouts from the health sector.

a896.speaker: Adrian Chikumbe, Ministry of Health spokesperson (Malawi)
a896.speech: Conceded that eliminating malaria by 2030 will be a tall order, especially with the recent trends showing an increase in both infections and deaths amid resource limitations; however, he said government is looking into ways of filling the gap created by US’s aid cuts towards the country’s health sector ; “Funding for malaria is still there, although it has been affected by cuts. We have other sources of funding. We also launched the National Health Financing Strategy, which suggests ways to fund the health sector, including paying services, medical schemes, engaging the corporate world to support health services.” ; also said the ministry is pushing for resources in the national budget to meet the Abuja Declaration of allocating 15 percent of total expenditure to the health sector.

a896.speaker: Health rights activists
a896.speech: Have urged government to step up efforts in eliminating the disease by 2030.

a896.speaker: George Jobe, Malawi Health Equity Network executive director
a896.speech: Said achieving the 2030 target will require stronger political will, sustained funding, and intensified community engagement and awareness raising; added that funding cuts by donors at a time malaria cases are increasing will heavily affect efforts against the disease ; “While Malawi has strong policies and a National Malaria Strategic Plan, the current surge in cases shows we should do more at the scale and intensity required. Prevention methods such as mosquito net distribution, indoor residual spraying, and environmental management are not reaching all households consistently. Community awareness and behaviour change campaigns also need strengthening.”

a896.speaker: Maziko Matemba, Health Rights Education Programme executive director
a896.speech: Described the rise in the malaria cases and resultant deaths as worrisome; emphasised that the country needs to invest more in malaria prevention.

a896.speaker: Lazarus Chakwera, President of Malawi
a896.speech: Described the disease as a threat that costs government dearly, saying it accounts for 36 percent of out-patient cases and 15 percent of all hospital admissions in the country.

a898.speaker: Economic analysts
a898.speech: Stressed that to counter the effects of the coronavirus pandemic will demand great determination in 2021, 2022 and beyond; said that planning for this challenging global future needs to start right now, even though we do not yet know the full degree of the pain that the world’s citizens and their economies are set to endure in the immediate period ahead.

a898.speaker: David Malpass, World Bank President
a898.speech: Estimates that up to 150 million people are being plunged into extreme poverty this year, taking the global total to well above 800 million.

a898.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a898.speech: Forecasts that the world’s economy will recover significantly in 2021 from its near-depression 2020 levels, and that the economic rebound will be due to the demise of the virus and the abundance of vaccines and effective treatments.

a898.speaker: Frank Vogl, Co-founder of Transparency International and author of “Waging War on Corruption”
a898.speech: Stated that the great unraveling embraces a failure of multilateral strategic decision-making at the highest levels, and that the Trump administration has led the charge as the great disrupter – attacking the World Health Organization, deriding the World Trade Organization, and failing to lead on multilateral financial responses.

a898.speaker: Frank Vogl, Co-founder of Transparency International
a898.speech: Noted that the onset of the global financial crisis in September 2008 saw the convening in less than two months of a Group of 20 summit meeting to determine collective international action, while this year the Group of Seven has been in hiding and the Finance Ministers of the G20 have only met to take minimal measures to kick the can down the road, calling merely for short-term deferrals in debt repayments by the world’s poorest countries.

a898.speaker: Frank Vogl, Co-founder of Transparency International
a898.speech: Stressed that the immediate multilateral response to this crisis has been swift: giant lending programs launched by the International Monetary Fund, and rapid disbursing loans and grants from the World Bank, with debt being piled upon debt across the universe.

a898.speaker: Frank Vogl, Co-founder of Transparency International
a898.speech: Stated that the financial resources of the IMF will need to be hugely expanded, that it has to develop systems to enable countries to stretch out their official debt servicing in return for being willing to be open to forceful IMF monitoring of exactly how the aid funds are used, and that the G7 needs to hold a special meeting to find ways to convince China to become part of the international “Paris Club” of official creditors and agree to making transparent its loan arrangements with dozens of countries.

a898.speaker: Lex Rieffel, Nonresident Fellow with the East Asia Program at the Stimson Center
a898.speech: Stated that public spending deficits are reaching record highs in many countries, but because interest rates are close to record lows central bankers tend to be relaxed about this and note that national debt service payments are quite low relative to overall government budget outlays; however, tens of millions of pensioners who depend on yields from their fixed income investments are likely to face financial hardship, and not a single government has yet addressed the financial distress of the elderly in high-income countries – a giant problem that may take a toll for years to come.

a898.speaker: Lex Rieffel, Nonresident Fellow, Stimson Center
a898.speech: Argued that with the pandemic destroying economies, emerging market countries desperately need more cash to service their existing outstanding debts; China is renegotiating some of its deals but keeping all details secret; the 75 lowest income countries are being allowed by the G20 to defer debt servicing until June 2021, while commercial creditors are not being generous, so IMF loans are being recycled by recipient countries to pay off the Chinese and commercial creditors while citizens receive scant relief.

a898.speaker: Lex Rieffel, Nonresident Fellow, Stimson Center
a898.speech: According to him, the G20, the IMF and the World Bank at the global level, just like the EU and U.S. authorities at the regional and national levels, are pouring unprecedented amounts of money at the immediate COVID 19 challenge, hoping that somehow there will never be a day of reckoning; these emergency responses are not only understandable, but laudable, and there are no alternatives.

a902.speaker: Authorities of the Grand Kru Technical College
a902.speech: Are pleading with local and international partners, including USAID, UNDP, UNESCO, the Chinese Embassy in Liberia, and the Government of Liberia, to help construct the building that will house the college in the county.

a902.speaker: Professor T. Dan Jah Bestman, Vice President for Administration, Grand Kru Technical College
a902.speech: Says the College needs about 12 million United States Dollars to construct its campus; said that about 50 acres of land have already been secured in Grand Kru County, and they need about Four Hundred Thousand United States Dollars ($400,000) to jump-start construction ; said the college does not have the mobility to transport materials to the county, thus it stocks equipment at its Monrovia office ; revealed that the College signed an MOU with the Ministry of Agriculture local office in the county to use its premises for about five years, but they fear that they may be thrown out as the Ministry of Agriculture embarks on strengthening its sub-offices across the country.

a902.speaker: Professor T. Dan Jah Bestman, Vice President for Administration, Grand Kru Technical College
a902.speech: Lauded the County Legislative Caucus and the Acting President of Grand Kru Technical College, Josephus M. Gray, for the level of support and cooperation they are receiving for the college’s forward match ; lauded the government and the Grand Kru County Legislative Caucus for transitioning from TEVT to Grand Kru Technical College (GKTC), which he noted is highly welcoming.

a902.speaker: Professor T. Dan Jah Bestman, Vice President for Administration, Grand Kru Technical College
a902.speech: Pointed out that the college currently has about 3,300 students for its first Semester of 2024/2025, surpassing Tubman University’s enrollment when it first opened in Maryland County in 2009.

a1013.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) (statement)
a1013.speech: Said Monday that the number of people experiencing crisis levels of hunger in Somalia is expected to rise to 4.4 million between October and December: "At least 3.6 million people are currently experiencing crisis levels of hunger in Somalia. This number is expected to rise to 4.4 million people between October and December when below average rains are anticipated" ; According to the statement, 1.6 million children under the age of five are at risk of acute malnutrition until July 2025 in Somalia, including 403,000 who are likely to suffer from severe malnutrition, representing a 14 and 21% increase in Global Acute Malnutrition and Severe Acute Malnutrition compared with the same period last year, with the expected deterioration largely attributable to the expected scale-down of humanitarian and social protection programs due to limited funding ; "This will likely lead to reduced health and nutrition services that are crucial to preventing or managing acute malnutrition, especially among the displaced population that rely heavily on humanitarian assistance," it added ; it also said the seasonal rise in disease prevalence and the potential outbreaks are expected to significantly exacerbate the situation, and that access to safe drinking water and sanitation facilities is expected to decline during the rainy season.

a1013.speaker: James Swan, UN acting envoy to Somalia
a1013.speech: On Oct. 3, called for further support to the $1.6 billion 2024 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan, which is only 37% funded.

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Presenting the budget framework proposal for the 2025/2026 fiscal year in Parliament, said that other priority areas include infrastructure development, strengthening productive sectors and improving social services, environmental management and climate change, enhancing institutional systems for good governance, and promoting gender equality and empowerment of special groups.

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Said that domestic revenue is projected at 38.9 tril/- compared to the 34.6tril/- projected for 2024/25, and listed the measures as promoting the use of ICT systems, controlling tax exemptions and improving the business and investment environment to unlock new revenue sources ; "The government's aim is to ensure that domestic revenue continues to fund a significant portion of the national budget, with at least 70 per cent of the total budget. The government will continue implementing a medium-term revenue collection strategy aimed at increasing domestic revenue and reducing reliance on loans and aid in the budget."

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Said that spending is expected to be 55.06tril/-, of which 38.6tril/- will be for recurrent expenditures and 16.4tril/- for development.

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Said the framework includes various directives for accounting officers to strictly follow, including prioritising the completion of ongoing projects before initiating new ones, settling debts of ongoing or completed projects, ensuring all collected revenue is deposited into the government's Consolidated Fund, use of the government payment system (MUSE) and electronic revenue collection systems, implementing the 2021 Guidelines on Requests and Disbursement of Funds, compliance with the Public Procurement Act, and adherence to contract agreements, tax laws and full project preparation ; "Implementing the national strategy to improve access to foreign currency, including controlling unnecessary foreign exchange use, boosting production of export goods and services, enhancing the business and investment environment to attract foreign capital and prioritising local goods and services will be stressed."

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Said there is a need for close monitoring of the performance of state-owned enterprises, particularly those operating commercially, with a strategy to prepare them for listing on the stock market to reduce the government's obligation to fund and manage them, and called for sectoral collaboration in implementing multi-sector projects, ensuring environmental and climate change considerations and addressing community needs.

a1092.speaker: Dr Mwigulu Nchemba, Minister for Finance of Tanzania
a1092.speech: Noted that in the first quarter of 2024/25 the government collected 11.5tril/- from all sources, of which 7.9tril/- came from domestic revenue, equivalent to 99.4 per cent of the target, while aid and concessional loans amounted to 1.37tril/-, commercial loans from the domestic market reached 1.6tril/- and commercial loans from external sources were 593.65bn/-.

a1181.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a1181.speech: Disclosed that his administration would be diverting from the previous economic policy approach that had been based on 'aggregate demand' to 'aggregate supply.' "For the past 15 years, we've been using 'big push' policy to drive the stagnated economy." ; "With this, lots of positive achievements were made based on aggregate demand."

a1181.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a1181.speech: "Our main aim will be controlling the inflationary pressure in the economy."

a1181.speaker: Getachew Asfaw, economist who has published books on the macroeconomic conditions of Ethiopia
a1181.speech: Said the aggregate demand approach is very common in most developing countries. "However, it has created income inequality, caused higher inflationary pressure in the economy and macroeconomic imbalances."

a1181.speaker: Getachew Asfaw, economist
a1181.speech: Shares Moody's assessment on political uncertainty: "The existing political uncertainty would have a negative impact on the economic growth of the country."

a1181.speaker: Getachew Asfaw, economist
a1181.speech: Said that the major problem of the government is bringing the plans down to earth. "They need to be practical in implementing what they promise and plan."

a1181.speaker: Alemayehu Geda (Prof.), macroeconomist and university lecturer
a1181.speech: Said that, given the double-digit inflation in the economy, the approved budget is not expansionary; is skeptical of the economic growth rate forecasted by the government and argues that in targeting tax revenue collection the government considers the forecasted economic growth, which is inflated, making revenue forecasts wrong. "Considering the situation in the country, the growth rate could not exceed seven percent." ; "The exaggerated forecast would have a negative impact on the target of tax revenue." ; "This will lead the government to request a supplementary budget." ; "The supplementary budget will push the inflationary pressure high."

a1181.speaker: Alemayehu Geda (Prof.), macroeconomist
a1181.speech: Says that inflation would stay in the double digits in the coming fiscal year.

a1181.speaker: Alemayehu Geda (Prof.), macroeconomist
a1181.speech: Said searching for a grant can be an option to escape from a budget deficit and a supplementary budget. "However, the grants have to be used for the procurement of essential goods like wheat, instead of injecting it into the economy, converting it into Birr." ; "If so, it could cause inflation."

a1181.speaker: Ministry of Finance of Ethiopia
a1181.speech: Has targeted the budget deficit to be 56.8 billion Br, lower by three billion Birr from the last fiscal year's target.

a1181.speaker: Moody's Investors Service (report)
a1181.speech: Reported that the political uncertainty in the country would be a challenge for the economy: "The new administration's efforts to embark on a set of wide-ranging reforms have intensified underlying political tensions, which risks derailing economic activity."

a1234.speaker: American generals and politicians
a1234.speech: had criticised Zelensky’s refusal to mobilise more men, considering that it jeopardised Ukraine’s chances of success.

a1234.speaker: Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a Washington-based think tank
a1234.speech: estimates that between 60,000 and 100,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed since the start of the war.

a1234.speaker: European officials
a1234.speech: share this concern and are worried about the lack of effort made by Kyiv to remedy the shortage of soldiers.

a1234.speaker: The Telegraph (British newspaper)
a1234.speech: reports that instead of increasing the number of volunteers, the policy change has fuelled a wave of migration.

a1234.speaker: AfD (German far-right party)
a1234.speech: demands an end to financial aid to Ukrainians.

a1234.speaker: Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert of the CDU (in Politico)
a1234.speech: said bluntly: “We have no interest in young Ukrainians spending their time in Germany instead of defending their country. Ukraine is free to make its own choices, but the recent change in the law has generated an emigration trend that we must deal with.”

a1462.speaker: Six sources familiar with the matter (anonymous)
a1462.speech: Told Reuters that President Donald Trump's administration on Tuesday moved to reinstate at least six recently canceled U.S. foreign aid programs for emergency food assistance.

a1462.speaker: Jeremy Lewin, USAID Acting Deputy Administrator (internal email)
a1462.speech: Asked staff in an internal email to reverse the terminations, asking to restore awards to the World Food Programme in Lebanon, Syria, Somalia, Jordan, Iraq and Ecuador, according to five sources familiar with the matter: "Sorry for all the back and forth on awards. There are a lot of stakeholders and we need to do better about balancing these competing interests — that's my fault and I take responsibility."

a1462.speaker: Reuters
a1462.speech: Reported on Monday that the Trump administration had ended life-saving aid programs for more than a dozen countries including Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia and Syria, totaling over $1.3 billion.

a1462.speaker: Stand Up For Aid, an advocacy group of current and former U.S. officials
a1462.speech: According to the group, WFP contracts canceled on Lewin's orders last weekend for Lebanon, Syria, Somalia and Jordan totaled more than $463 million.

a1462.speaker: US State Department
a1462.speech: Said the waivers granted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio to many of the terminated programs following an initial round of cuts did not reflect a final decision.

a1462.speaker: US State Department
a1462.speech: Did not immediately respond to a request for comment about restoring the awards.

a1462.speaker: Two sources (anonymous)
a1462.speech: Said the decision to restore some aid followed pressure from inside the administration and from Congress.

a1462.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a1462.speech: Said on Monday that the U.S. notified the organization it was eliminating emergency food assistance funding in 14 countries, warning: "If implemented, this could amount to a death sentence for millions of people facing extreme hunger and starvation."

a1462.speaker: Tammy Bruce, US State Department spokesperson
a1462.speech: Told reporters on Tuesday that the United States had concerns that WFP funding for Yemen and Afghanistan was benefiting the Houthis and the Taliban; "There were a few programs that were cut in other countries that were not meant to be cut that have been rolled back and put into place," Bruce said, adding that the administration remains committed to foreign aid.

a1462.speaker: US officials (anonymous)
a1462.speech: Described the overhaul under which the administration has canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid since the start of Trump's second term as marked by chaos and confusion.

a1462.speaker: Senate Foreign Relations Committee Democrats (letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio)
a1462.speech: Wrote a letter to Rubio on Tuesday regarding plans to restructure the State Department, including by folding in USAID, which they said was "unconstitutional, illegal, unjustified, damaging, and inefficient."

a1555.speaker: Benjamin Okezie Kalu, Deputy Speaker of Nigeria's House of Representatives and Chair of the Monetary and Financial Affairs Committee of the Pan-African Parliament
a1555.speech: Has called for urgent global action to address Africa's mounting debt crisis, advocating for debt cancellation mechanisms and the renegotiation of trade agreements with the European Union (EU), and emphasized the need for reforms that prioritize development and economic justice, especially through debt-for-development swaps and alignment of the EU-Africa Economic Partnership Agreements (EPAs) with the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). “This partnership offers a timely and transformative opportunity to reshape EU-Africa parliamentary relations through the lens of justice, equity, and structural change, a relationship built on mutual respect, sustainable development, and shared values.” ; “Our key areas of collaboration will also focus on EU-AU joint advocacy for debt cancellation mechanisms, including debt-for-development swaps, and parliamentary oversight on African countries either in debt distress or at high risk of it. This signals the urgent need for reforms in global debt governance.”

a1555.speaker: Benjamin Okezie Kalu, Deputy Speaker of Nigeria's House of Representatives
a1555.speech: Stressed the importance of reforming the current trade architecture by aligning the EPAs with AfCFTA protocols, supporting Africa's industrialization goals, and eliminating non-tariff barriers that stifle local manufacturing. “With only 15% of Africa's trade being intra-continental while 80% of exports are still raw commodities, there's an urgent need to incorporate value chain localization, intellectual property protection, and industrial policy space into these trade agreements.”

a1555.speaker: Benjamin Okezie Kalu, Deputy Speaker of Nigeria's House of Representatives
a1555.speech: Urged the creation of a joint EU-AU working group to combat illicit financial flows (IFFs) from the continent: “Africa loses over $88 billion annually to illicit financial flows—almost twice the amount it receives in official development assistance. There must be collaborative efforts toward African asset recovery, BEPS compliance, and enhanced EU transparency obligations.”

a1555.speaker: Benjamin Okezie Kalu, Deputy Speaker of Nigeria's House of Representatives
a1555.speech: Stressed the need for Africa to be recognized as a strategic partner in the global green transition: “Despite being the most vulnerable continent to climate change, Africa receives only 3% of global climate finance. We advocate for unconditional climate finance and a robust EU-AU monitoring mechanism to ensure transparency in implementation.” ; noted that although Africa holds 60% of the world's solar energy potential, it receives less than 1% of global solar investment — “This stark imbalance must be corrected through scaled-up investments in solar infrastructure and African-led energy solutions tailored to local needs.” ; insisted that the EU Green Deal must align with Africa's Agenda 2063, particularly around climate adaptation, renewable energy access, and the operationalisation of the Loss and Damage Fund.

a1555.speaker: Benjamin Okezie Kalu, Deputy Speaker of Nigeria's House of Representatives
a1555.speech: On migration, emphasized the importance of addressing its root causes, including conflict, youth unemployment, and climate stress, while promoting legal mobility and skills development: “Empowering local economies will reduce the economic push factors that drive irregular migration. A holistic approach must expand legal pathways for mobility, including talent mobility initiatives such as Erasmus+, digital nomad visas, and intra-company transfers.” ; “Ultimately, creating high-value jobs in Africa, particularly in sectors like digital services, green industries, and manufacturing, presents the most sustainable and dignified alternative to irregular migration.”

a1555.speaker: Levinus Nwabughiogu, Chief Press Secretary to the Deputy Speaker (statement)
a1555.speech: In a statement issued, Kalu was quoted as saying that parliamentary collaboration between Africa and Europe must move beyond traditional donor-recipient dynamics and instead focus on shared prosperity and inclusive policies.

a1555.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB) 2024 statistics
a1555.speech: Cited by Kalu as the source for the figures that only 15% of Africa's trade is intra-continental while 80% of exports are still raw commodities.

a2137.speaker: Jose Antonio Ocampo, professor at Columbia University (commentary provided by Project Syndicate)
a2137.speech: Observed that the recent UN and G20 summits have highlighted a concerning truth that the world is moving too slowly on crucial fronts like ending poverty and ensuring food security. ; Argued that international development financing must be expanded significantly; that developing countries need more support to enable them to contribute to the provision of global goods, particularly the fight against global pandemics and climate change, and manage the effects of international economic disruptions; and that some form of relief must be provided to countries at high risk of debt stress, a group that includes at least one-third of developing economies. ; Noted that high-income countries are falling short of the official development assistance goals set by the UN a half-century ago and have often failed to contribute as much as expected to special funds, so convincing them to finance these new initiatives will be difficult.

a2137.speaker: G20 Leaders' Declaration (New Delhi summit)
a2137.speech: Offered little more than an affirmation that the G20 stands by the commitments made in the Common Framework for Debt Treatment Beyond the DSSI.

a2137.speaker: UN's Africa Group
a2137.speech: Tabled a resolution to create an intergovernmental committee to draft the Terms of References for a UN Framework Convention on Tax Cooperation, given the OECD Inclusive Framework's perceived weak benefits for developing countries.

a2137.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a2137.speech: Predicts that global growth will be low in 2023 (three percent) and 2024 (2.9pc) - compared to 3.7pc per year in the decade before the pandemic - with both developed and developing countries struggling. ; Recommends that central banks take a cautious approach to interest rates, lowering them only when inflation is fully under control.

a2165.speaker: Andrei Belousov, Russian Minister of Defence
a2165.speech: "I consider our meeting today as a new stage in the development of our friendly relations." For him, this meeting is an opportunity for the two countries to revisit and strengthen bilateral cooperation between Russia and Burkina Faso.

a2165.speaker: Apollinaire Joachimson Kyelem de Tambela, Prime Minister of Burkina Faso
a2165.speech: Raised the possibility of an increase in the contingent of Russian military instructors in Burkina Faso. He stressed that Burkina Faso needs more weapons, especially ones suited to fighting terrorism and defending its sovereignty. He also recalled that "Russia is an ideal partner in the fight against terrorism" while noting Russia's capacity to "stand up to the West as a military power."

a2165.speaker: Alexander Novak, Russian Deputy Prime Minister
a2165.speech: According to the Russian Deputy Prime Minister, the trade turnover between Burkina Faso and Russia increased fivefold between January and July 2024 compared with the same period the previous year.

a2165.speaker: Russia
a2165.speech: Russia committed to maintaining humanitarian and food aid to Burkina Faso, in particular medicines, epidemic-control equipment and cereals.

a2236.speaker: Joseph Onojaeme, Delta State Commissioner for Health
a2236.speech: Disclosed at the flag-off of the Maternal and Neonatal Mortality Reduction Innovation and Initiatives Project that the state government had sacked some health workers who allegedly extorted pregnant women and children under five, and said the ministry had intensified monitoring of hospitals to ensure that funds released for maternal and child healthcare were properly utilised: "Health workers in the state have done well, but in every 12, there is a Judas. We have received reports of some collecting money from pregnant women and children under five for drugs, while still forwarding the bills to the government for payment." ; "We have demoted some of these fraudulent workers and sacked many within this short period. With continuous monitoring and the support of mothers, these practices will reduce." ; stressed that the state covers the medical expenses of all pregnant women until delivery and provides free treatment for children under five.

a2236.speaker: Joseph Onojaeme, Delta State Commissioner for Health
a2236.speech: Urged residents to report any health worker demanding payment for maternal or child care, noting that the phone number of the executive assistant to the governor on health monitoring would be made public for such reports.

a2236.speaker: Joseph Onojaeme, Delta State Commissioner for Health
a2236.speech: Revealed that the state's maternal mortality rate had dropped from over 200 to less than 120 per 100,000 live births, expressing optimism that the Maternal and Neonatal Mortality Reduction Innovation and Initiatives Project would further reduce the figures.

a2236.speaker: John Ovuoraye, representative of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a2236.speech: Reaffirmed the federal government's commitment to supporting states in lowering maternal and neonatal deaths, and said 172 local government areas across 33 states had been identified as high-risk zones, including five in Delta - Ndokwa East, Ughelli North, Aniocha North, Udu, and Sapele.

a2236.speaker: John Ovuoraye, representative of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a2236.speech: Said that the Maternal and Neonatal Mortality Reduction Innovation and Initiatives Project, supported by President Bola Tinubu, is being implemented in collaboration with USAID, WHO, UNICEF, the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the World Bank, and several European partners.

a2236.speaker: Francis Nwifuru, Governor of Ebonyi State
a2236.speech: In November 2024 ordered the arrest and prosecution of six health workers for allegedly selling and diverting materials meant for the state's Ministry of Health ; later suspended Moses Ekuma, the state health commissioner, for three months for not showing the "capacity" to manage the ministry.

a2509.speaker: Peter H. Vrooman, U.S. Ambassador to Mozambique
a2509.speech: "This bi-partisan congressional delegation visit to Mozambique is yet another example of the multi-dimensional U.S.-Mozambique friendship and partnership, which spans decades."

a2509.speaker: Senator Christopher Coons (D-DE)
a2509.speech: "It was great to discuss cooperation on economic development, countering violent extremism, and international conservation with our partners in Mozambique. Mozambique is at the forefront of the U.S. Strategy for Sub-Saharan Africa."

a2509.speaker: US Department of State (@StateDept post)
a2509.speech: "The U.S. recognizes that Sub-Saharan Africa plays a critical role in advancing global priorities to the benefit of Africans and Americans. That is why we are building on our actions and commitments to deepen our engagement and partnerships in Africa."

a2509.speaker: U.S. Embassy in Mozambique (@USEmbassyMaputo post)
a2509.speech: Posted that a delegation of U.S. congress members led by @ChrisCoons visited Bazaruto National Park to learn about U.S. efforts in assistance for environmental conservation that boosts tourism, generates jobs and mitigates the effects of climate change.

a2509.speaker: Senator Rob Portman (R-OH) (@senrobportman post)
a2509.speech: "Our countries have a shared interest in strong governance and increasing the stability of Mozambique, as well as the development of their vast natural resources, which will help bring greater energy security to the county and world."

a2509.speaker: Senator Rob Portman (R-OH) (@senrobportman post)
a2509.speech: "We discussed ways to strengthen cooperation between our countries and support greater economic development through targeted security assistance to support the responsible development of Mozambique's natural gas resources."

a2509.speaker: Meg Whitman, U.S. Ambassador to Kenya (@USAmbKenya posts)
a2509.speech: "Fantastic to welcome the Senator @ChrisCoons-led delegation to [Kenya], the third stop on a five country Africa visit!" ; "The delegation is also scheduled to meet with President Kenyatta, @WilliamsRuto, and @RailaOdinga to discuss shared goals - health, security, and economic prosperity. #USKEPartnership"

a2615.speaker: Rumbidzai Kabasa, Provincial Magistrate (court ruling)
a2615.speech: Convicted Tavonga Ticharwa (43) of Nyaradza, Gokwe, of culpable homicide for the death of the unidentified victim; the court ordered the truck driver to pay a US$400 fine, with an alternative sentence of six months in prison if the fine is not paid.

a2615.speaker: Wisdom Shava, prosecutor
a2615.speech: According to the prosecutor, on November 29, 2024, around 10pm, Ticharwa was driving a Freightliner truck loaded with 30 tonnes of coal from Victoria Falls to Bulawayo with no passengers on board; during a brief stop at the Hwange Truck Stop, Ticharwa got out to relieve himself, unaware that an unknown pedestrian had crawled under the truck and fallen asleep; Ticharwa got back into the truck, started the engine, and drove off without checking underneath the vehicle, running over the sleeping man, who died instantly.

a2615.speaker: Police (records from the scene)
a2615.speech: Police at the scene noted bloodstains on the truck’s three left rear outer axle wheels; the victim’s body was taken to Colliery Hospital mortuary, where a post-mortem examination was later conducted at United Bulawayo Hospitals.

a2615.speaker: The State (prosecution)
a2615.speech: Argued that Ticharwa was negligent in failing to properly inspect around and under the vehicle before driving off.

a2814.speaker: Donald Trump, U.S. President
a2814.speech: said on Wednesday that his administration's cuts to the U.S. Agency for International Development and its aid programs worldwide have been "devastating." "It's devastating, and hopefully a lot of people are going to start spending a lot of money." ; "I've talked to other nations. We want them to chip in and spend money too, and we've spent a lot. And it's a big - it's a tremendous problem going on in many countries. A lot of problems going on. The United States always gets the request for money. Nobody else helps."

a2814.speaker: U.S. State Department
a2814.speech: The State Department, which manages USAID, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

a2814.speaker: Trump administration
a2814.speech: has repeatedly defended the cuts, saying they were focused on wasted funds.

a2814.speaker: U.S. government data
a2814.speech: The United States disbursed $61 billion in foreign assistance last year, just over half of it via USAID, according to government data; the U.S. spent half a billion dollars on South African aid in 2023, mostly on healthcare, the most recent data shows.

a2814.speaker: Reuters
a2814.speech: has reported that in the months since the cuts, testing and monitoring of HIV patients across South Africa has decreased.

a2889.speaker: Research by IFPRI (International Food Policy Research Institute)
a2889.speech: Found that such controls distorted markets and drove smuggling across borders.

a2889.speaker: World Bank
a2889.speech: In Zambia, export restrictions proved "counterproductive," according to the World Bank. They undermined rural incomes and deterred investment, as farmers could not plan for future markets.

a2955.speaker: George Conway, Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia
a2955.speech: Called on all parties to protect civilians and humanitarian workers in areas of conflict: “The World Humanitarian Day theme for this year, #ActForHumanity, urges the world to do a better job of protecting civilians and humanitarians, especially in conflict zones. It implores us to reflect and honour aid workers, who around the world, are targeted or obstructed as they work to help people in need.” ; “On this day, every year, we shine a spotlight on humanitarian workers and the millions of civilians around the world whose lives have been caught up in humanitarian crises. I pay particular tribute to Somali aid workers who, despite immense challenges, have demonstrated their commitment to serve those in most need of assistance and protection.”

a2955.speaker: George Conway, Deputy Special Representative of the Secretary-General, UN Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator for Somalia
a2955.speech: “Authorities and non-state armed groups have clear and long-established international legal obligations in conflict, including to protect civilians from harm, spare schools and hospitals and ensure the safe passage of humanitarian workers. Every time these rules are broken, human suffering intensifies and civilians are pushed into greater despair. Every time these lines are crossed, humanitarian needs grow.”

a3311.speaker: United States / U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) (announcement)
a3311.speech: Announces a new program to provide information on climate change advocacy tools for persons with disabilities in Mozambique. The goal of this project is to make information about emergency preparedness and climate change systems accessible to those who are blind, deaf, or other forms of disability.

a3311.speaker: UNICEF
a3311.speech: According to UNICEF, persons with disabilities are usually left out of discussions about policies, plans, and programs that prepare communities for and respond to these climate events at the national and subnational level.

a3311.speaker: Helen Pataki, USAID Mission Director
a3311.speech: “The United States is dedicated to helping all people with disabilities to participate actively in Mozambique’s public life. Inclusivity improves decision-making and strengthens communities.”

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star and author of African Uhuru
a3499.speech: Said Africa must refuse to repay illegitimate debt and demand reparations from former colonial powers and corporations; described Africa's US$1.5 trillion debt as "neo-enslavement" and a deliberate tool of control maintained by global financial institutions; said more than 30 African countries now spend more on debt repayments than healthcare, calling this a manufactured dependency designed to maintain Africa's economic weakness. "This is not development. This is a system built to keep us dependent. If the World Bank and IMF refuse to cancel Africa's odious debt, then Africa should simply refuse to pay." ; citing precedents such as Ecuador and Argentina, which defaulted on illegitimate debts and recovered, he urged African leaders to take coordinated action against what he called a predatory global financial system.

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star
a3499.speech: Said Africa's economic crisis is inseparable from the historical legacy of slavery, colonialism, and resource extraction: "It is not Africa that owes Europe - it is Europe that owes Africa." ; referenced the British government's compensation of slave owners in 1833 and the continued economic exclusion of African descendants of slavery: "This grotesque reversal of justice must be corrected. Reparations are not a handout. They are a debt long overdue."

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star
a3499.speech: Said corporations that profited from slavery and colonialism must be held accountable; he singled out Lloyd's of London, which insured slave ships and issued an apology in 2020, calling such statements insufficient: "These companies are sitting on the compounded interest of centuries of theft. If they were serious, they would transfer wealth."

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star
a3499.speech: Linked Africa's debt and historical exploitation to the climate crisis, noting that the continent is among the least responsible for global emissions but bears a disproportionate share of climate-related disasters and food insecurity: "Climate reparations are as essential as financial reparations." ; criticised the structure of international climate negotiations, arguing that they routinely sideline Africa's interests: "We cannot remain in an abusive relationship and keep coping with it. We must walk away and rebuild global engagement on our terms."

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star
a3499.speech: Outlined specific measures that reparations should include, such as debt cancellation, the return of looted artefacts, windfall taxes on companies that benefited from slavery and colonisation, and investment in African-led development strategies; said Africa has the capacity to lead its own development and does not need to rely on external models or validation; called for the establishment of scholarship and trust funds for the descendants of the enslaved and condemned the refusal of European institutions to return stolen cultural property, calling it "deeply racist and indefensible."

a3499.speaker: Roger McKenzie, international editor of the Morning Star
a3499.speech: Concluded: "There will be no Harriet Tubman figure to rescue us this time. Liberation will come only through collective struggle - by us, for us."

a3527.speaker: Dr Philip Mpango, Vice President of Tanzania (speaking on behalf of President Samia Suluhu Hassan)
a3527.speech: Has called on religious leaders across the country to strengthen their collaboration with the government in order to better serve the people and address pressing societal challenges; stressed the importance of unity between the state and faith-based institutions: “It is vital that the government and religious organisations work more closely together to counter misleading theologies, fight poverty, protect the environment and navigate interfaith challenges” ; reassured delegates that the government remains committed to protecting freedom of worship and spiritual expression for all Tanzanians, while upholding peace, stability and national unity.

a3527.speaker: Dr Philip Mpango, Vice President of Tanzania
a3527.speech: Urged UEM delegates to focus their discussions on urgent global concerns, especially environmental conservation and sustainable development, saying that these issues affect all life on Earth, not just people, but also plants and animals; “Scientific reports clearly show that, by 2030, humanity could face serious threats if we fail to act on environmental degradation, climate change and pollution,” he warned.

a3527.speaker: Dr Philip Mpango, Vice President of Tanzania
a3527.speech: Encouraged churches and religious missions to increase investment in social service projects, particularly in education, healthcare and support for vulnerable populations; noted that such investments reduce dependency on foreign aid and build more self-reliant communities ; praised the ELCT for its ongoing support to people with disabilities, including children and those living with mental health conditions, saying the Church’s efforts have significantly contributed to the inclusion and empowerment of these often-marginalised groups ; “I urge the Church to expand these essential services. Our communities still have unmet needs, especially among people with special needs.”

a3545.speaker: Nabil Ayouch, Moroccan film director of “Everybody Loves Touda”
a3545.speech: Expressed his pride at representing Morocco in an international competition of this scale: “It is an honour for all of us and an opportunity to show the vitality of Moroccan, and more broadly African, cinema on the world stage,” he told the press.

a4197.speaker: Sources at USAID (U.S. Agency for International Development)
a4197.speech: Confirmed that PEPFAR is included in the suspension of funding, although the order did not specifically name it.

a4197.speaker: Jeremy Konyndyk, former senior USAID official
a4197.speech: Warned that the halt to PEPFAR would be catastrophic for nations like Malawi: “The immediate cessation of funding will disrupt life-saving programs and endanger the health of millions” ; “For people living with HIV in Malawi, this freeze could halt their access to vital treatment, leading to avoidable deaths and further transmission of the virus.”

a4197.speaker: Asia Russell, executive director of the HIV access organization Health GAP
a4197.speech: Described the decision as “catastrophic” for countries like Malawi: “This freeze does not just affect funding for the future—it halts ongoing programs that are keeping people alive” ; “The impact will be immediate and devastating.”

a4399.speaker: Dr. Hassan Mohamed Hussein (Muungaab), Governor of Banadir Regional Administration and Mayor of Mogadishu
a4399.speech: Welcomed the Ambassador with fraternal protocol and emphasised the longstanding importance of Turkey-Somalia relations in supporting the reconstruction, security, and development of the capital city ; underscored Turkey's pivotal role since 2011 in humanitarian assistance, as well as the continuation of a strategic partnership that includes infrastructure reconstruction, military training, counter-terrorism, social service development, and major projects such as the establishment of a satellite base ; pledged that the Banadir Regional Administration remains committed to facilitating Turkish investment and development initiatives in Mogadishu and expressed the municipality's interest in building cooperation and exchanging experiences with major Turkish cities to enhance essential services such as sanitation, road networks, sewage systems, firefighting, and emergency response.

a4399.speaker: Alper Aktas, Turkish Ambassador to Somalia
a4399.speech: Reaffirmed his country's steadfast and unconditional support for Somalia's state-building, peace-building, and development efforts ; expressed Turkey's commitment to assisting Somalia in advancing its democratic agenda, particularly preparations for the One Person, One Vote elections in Mogadishu and across the regions.

a4449.speaker: Lionel Zinsou, Prime Minister of Benin and candidate in the 6 March presidential election
a4449.speech: "The company Cajaf-Comon engages in unfair competition against local broiler chicken producers and leaves them unable to sell their products."

a4449.speaker: Ganiou Soglo, former minister of youth, sports and leisure, son of President Nicephore Soglo
a4449.speech: During an interview given to the press on Friday 12 February, dismantled Lionel Zinsou's untruths about the importation of frozen products in relation to local producers: "It is not enough to sit in an air-conditioned office to make such statements. It is because local broiler chicken production is not sufficient that Mr Sebastien Ajavon imports frozen products. If the Beninese State supported local producers, we would not be in this situation. Why is it that since 2006, when Lionel Zinsou became adviser to the head of state, he has done nothing and proposed nothing to support these producers?"

a4449.speaker: Ganiou Soglo, former minister of youth, sports and leisure, son of President Nicephore Soglo
a4449.speech: Pointed out: "Lionel Zinsou worked for a company that owns the Danone company (a French firm, world leader in fresh dairy products) in Benin. That company produces yoghurts. But curiously, Danone competes with local yoghurt producers such as Comtesse. Why does Lionel Zinsou say nothing about that? It is too easy to play the intellectual. It is understandable - it is French interests that matter to him."

a4510.speaker: Kpotozounmè Dè Hakpon III, King of Porto-Novo (Benin)
a4510.speech: Confided that he had continued negotiations, begun eight years earlier with the managers of an American brewery called "Hapoon", so that the brewery would also be set up in Benin ; according to his own words, he was well received by the brewery's managers and was also decorated ; gave the reasons why he wishes the brewery to be established in Benin, explaining that the brewery's name is almost identical to the name of his descendants, "Hakpon".

a4638.speaker: Edward Quirmolue, FAO Head of Animal Program
a4638.speech: Stressed the strong collaboration between the entity, USAID, the Agriculture Ministry, and the University of Liberia. "The initiative is to strengthen Liberia's animal health system and improve food security to address the critical shortage of veterinary para-professionals."

a4638.speaker: Layli Maparyan, President of the University of Liberia
a4638.speech: Emphasized the importance of the country's agricultural and veterinary education. "The program would provide practical skills critical to the growth of Liberia's livestock and farming sectors." ; Praised all the stakeholders, including the FAO, USAID, and the Agriculture Ministry, for their support in advancing agricultural education in Liberia ; Urged students to seize the opportunity and become agents of change, benefiting both their careers and their communities.

a4638.speaker: Solomon Hedd-Williams, Deputy Agriculture Minister for Technical Services
a4638.speech: Stressed the critical need for collaborative efforts to tackle food security, enhance animal health, and empower local economies. "The partnership demonstrates the capabilities of the UL and reflects the transformative power of education."

a4642.speaker: Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) (statement)
a4642.speech: Sharply criticized South African President Cyril Ramaphosa for allegedly breaching diplomatic protocols after contacting billionaire Elon Musk regarding the recently enacted Expropriation Act; labeled Ramaphosa's actions as "reckless," accusing him of compromising South Africa's sovereignty to appease U.S. interests; expressed dismay over Ramaphosa's direct engagement with Musk, an unelected U.S. business figure. "This breaking of diplomatic protocol should never be taken lightly" - describing it as symptomatic of a "dependency syndrome" on Western influence.

a4642.speaker: Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) (statement)
a4642.speech: Accused Musk of exploiting his ties with former U.S. President Donald Trump to pressure South African authorities into easing regulatory barriers for his satellite company, Starlink, saying Musk's push undermines South Africa's Broad-Based Black Economic Empowerment (B-BBEE) policy, which mandates that foreign-owned satellite firms allocate at least 30% ownership to historically disadvantaged South Africans.

a4642.speaker: Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) (statement)
a4642.speech: Criticized Ramaphosa's inconsistency, noting that just days earlier the government reprimanded Minister Gwede Mantashe for diplomatic missteps when he threatened to restrict mineral exports to the U.S. over foreign aid disputes.

a4642.speaker: Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) (statement)
a4642.speech: "The President's conduct risks opening the door to state capture" - drawing parallels to South Africa's troubled past with the Gupta family during Jacob Zuma's administration; urged Ramaphosa to avoid relying on foreign billionaires to shape national policy, stressing the importance of upholding diplomatic protocols and protecting South Africa's sovereignty.

a4707.speaker: Healthcare staff (Zambezi Region facilities)
a4707.speech: Expressed gratitude for the progress achieved through support from USAID, as these initiatives have significantly enhanced service delivery and health outcomes in the region.

a4712.speaker: Management of SBEE (Benin national electricity distribution company)
a4712.speech: Explained the real causes of the power cuts: that Benin and Togo pooled the management of their electricity sub-sector problems, giving rise to the CEB, which took over the generation and transmission of electrical energy in the two countries; that because investments in the electricity sub-sector are heavy, the two countries relieved the CEB of the generation segment and entrusted it to the private sector, leading to the construction of Contour Global in Togo by a private operator and of the Maria-Gleta power plant in Benin through the national budget; that with the arrival of President Boni Yayi in 2006 there was a new vision - without electricity, no development - so that all localities of Benin which had power from 6 p.m. to midnight were connected to the CEB interconnected network and now have electricity 24 hours a day, and demand exploded; that demand has also exploded across the sub-region, where only 5 ECOWAS countries hold nearly 88% of the sub-region's energy network, Nigeria alone more than 50%, so that sub-regional cooperation must be encouraged, which led to the creation of the West African Power Pool headquartered in Benin; that the government of Benin has put in place an emergency energy plan to supplement energy imported from Nigeria in the event of a total collapse of the network, with many contracts signed; that consumers are classified in two categories, the first category (the Presidency, the Head of State's residence, hospitals performing major operations, hotels of more than four storeys, airports, centres holding sensitive medical products such as vaccines) which must never lack power and must have a back-up source, and the second category which may also provide a back-up source if it judges it necessary; and that with solar kits many of these problems can be solved, with 45 megawatts of solar to be installed through the MCC project, concluding that the future of the electricity sub-sector in countries like Benin lies in regional cooperation and in self-sufficiency through renewable energy sources such as hydroelectricity, wind and solar.

a4722.speaker: Hon. Kim, East African Community (EAC) lawmaker
a4722.speech: Clarified that Kenya's recent visa policy will impose charges only on individuals who overstay their visas for more than three months, with a similar policy applying to Kenyans who overstay in South Sudan ; according to him, all citizens of member states are entitled to a free, three-month stay in any EAC country, which can be renewed either by leaving the country or applying for an extension at an immigration office ; "All visas entering each partner state should be within three months once the three months have expired you have to exit the country and re-enter the country in which you will be given the free visa and three months again" ; "Those who overstayed for more than three months and did not exit are people who are going to be charged that fee" ; "The government of Kenya is not the only one who imposes that fee on the citizens of South Sudan even our government also imposes those fees when Kenyans overstay in South Sudan."

a4722.speaker: Hon. Kim, East African Community (EAC) lawmaker
a4722.speech: Is now encouraging South Sudanese students and residents to visit the nearest immigration office to obtain a free resident permit: "If you are a resident you have the right to visit the nearest immigration office you will get a free resident permit, and also those who are studying in the EAC member state have been given student visas for one year" ; "Those charges are just on those who are entering to come and visit.
